A bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana was urged by Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Authority, that a special bench headed by Justice Vikram Nath asked it to set up shelters, which have to constructed by local authorities.
The solicitor general said the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) had been directed to establish shelter homes for stray cattle across the country, which, according to the Authority, would involve an expenditure of approximately Rs 7,000 crore.
"Our case is that it should be done by the local district-level administration. We cannot do it pan India," he said.

articles.title: SP Group backs Tata Sons listing
articles.summary: Mumbai: The Shapoorji Pallonji (SP) Group is backing a Tata Sons listing after a proposed 2.5% stake sale to monetise part of its holding was delayed, people familiar with the matter said. The SP Group, which owns about 18.37% of Tata Sons, had discussed the sale with Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata, with a tax-efficient structure involving a bank or financial institution being explored.The proposal stalled at Tata Sons and was formally taken to board only after the RBI's directive brought a listing requirement into focus, the people said.Also Read: Tata’s rival camps lawyer up ahead of looming legal battleThe discussions focused on a limited stake sale rather than an immediate broader monetisation and the proposal envisaged cash proceeds being paid to the SP Group over a defined period, potentially allowing Tata Sons to avoid a listing, the people said. SP Group and Tata Trusts did not comment.The last discussion on the matter with Tata Sons involved Noel Tata suggesting that separate teams from both sides be created to examine the monetisation proposal, the people said. The monetisation plan discussed earlier was being handled by Farokh Subedar on behalf of Tata Trusts, Ankur Verma representing Tata Sons, and a representative from the SP Group, sources said.Also Read: Tata Trusts says Chandrasekaran reappointment resolution was invalid, rejects casting-vote argumentSP Group chairman Shapoor Mistry had publicly backed the listing and said he looked forward to working constructively with Tata Sons on way forward.The SP Group's backing of a listing now gives the conglomerate another potential route to monetise its stake. A public listing could provide a market-based valuation for its holding and make it easier to attract an investor for part of the stake before an IPO, experts said."The SP Group holds just over 18% of Tata Sons and its intent has been to monetise part of this holding in some form," said Ketan Dalal, founder of Katalyst Advisors. "With the IPO now seeming very likely, monetising through an OFS or post IPO, of course, is one possibility." Post-listing lock-in requirements would need to be considered, he said. "Pricing issues would play an important part, both from the investor point of view and from the SP Group point of view. In any case, it is not a situation of one or the other, but it could be a combination of both routes," Dalal said.An earlier proposal in July involved a share swap under which SP Group would receive shares in a basket of listed Tata companies in exchange for part of its Tata Sons holding. Tata Sons chairman N Chandrasekaran had announced in early August that he would not seek reappointment when his term ended in February 2027 and did not participate in subsequent discussions.But he reversed his exit decision and agreed to continue as executive chairman of Tata Sons for another five years after Tata Sons board approved his reappointment on September 17.The SP Group's Tata Sons stake is held through Sterling Investments Corp and Cyrus Investments and has been pledged against borrowings. The group completed a ₹21,500 crore refinancing in July after telling investors it planned to monetise part of its Tata Sons holding through a listing or share sale within 18 months. articles.title: Bengal's industry push needs clear intent
articles.summary: Under BJP, West Bengal is once again debating how to put land together for industry. The debate has now acquired a distinctly technical vocabulary: acquisition, negotiated purchase and land pooling.The three mechanisms are not interchangeable. Acquisition involves compulsory purchase under a statutory framework. Negotiated purchase relies on agreement between landowner and purchaser. Land pooling allows owners to contribute land to a development scheme and receive a smaller, but serviced, and potentially more valuable plot in return. The choice, as recent policy discussions suggest, should depend on the nature of the project.Also Read: Picasso, Omega, Prithvi and Cats: A Mumbai journey through books, unexpected encounters and theatreFor Bengal, the question of land has always been inseparable from the question of industrialisation. So, the new discussion raises a more fundamental question: even if Bengal succeeds in solving the problem of industrial land, will it succeed in attracting capital? Land can be assembled through legislation, negotiation or planning. But capital can only be attracted through confidence.Excitement surrounding political change is understandable. Bengal has always regarded politics not merely as a mechanism of governance but also as a form of public entertainment. Movement of legislators from one camp to another has become a spectator sport.Also Read: Pass the buck to RBI, banks: Let the savings from digital payments fund UPI costs, not consumersCapital, however, follows a different script. It's largely indifferent to the daily theatre of politics, and far more concerned with the stability of institutions. Consider an entrepreneur planning a large investment. The questions are surprisingly simple. Not whether the government is Left, Right or Centre. Not whether ministers speak Bengali, Hindi or English. Not whether people will eat veg or non-veg food. Not whether one political camp will replace another in controlling campuses, institutions or public spaces. The real question is: will rules that exist today survive tomorrow? That confidence in the durability of institutions is what economists and investors describe as institutional credibility.It is in this context that the new government's willingness to reconsider how industrial land is assembled becomes significant. Bengal has already begun examining land pooling, industrial parks, and changes to landholding and land-utilisation rules. The government is also considering ways of making large contiguous parcels available without directly acquiring individual agricultural plots.This is important because Bengal's problem is not simply a shortage of land. It's a shortage of large, contiguous and legally usable parcels of land. Fragmented holdings, overlapping claims and restrictions on land use can make an apparently simple industrial project extraordinarily complicated.134372690Earlier attempts to create land banks from idle public sector land ran into precisely this problem: available parcels were often too small or too fragmented for large investors. Indeed, there are now signs of movement from policy to implementation. The government has cleared land for 33 industries, and that the land will be handed over before Durga Puja. This is significant. But the real test will be whether these allocations translate into timely project execution, employment and sustained private investment.Land pooling could be a useful solution. But it's not a magic wand. Bengal has laws that allow land to be reorganised for development. What matters now is whether these provisions can be implemented effectively, with clear rules on ownership, compensation, infrastructure and land use. Land pooling may bring plots together. But it cannot make ownership disputes disappear.And this is where the land question meets the question of capital. Corruption is costly. But uncertainty can be even more so. Investors can price an unofficial cost. It's much harder to price changing rules, administrative discretion and unpredictable policy.There's also a geographical reality. Large, contiguous parcels are rarely available near Bengal's major cities. So, industry may have to move farther out, where land disputes and infrastructure gaps can be greater. Industrialists, therefore, need to look beyond quick returns and become partners in building these new industrial regions with the government. Given Bengal's political history, industrialisation cannot be reduced to capitalist extraction alone. It must also create a stake for local communities.Capital has no ideology. But it has an excellent memory. Two decades ago, large sections of Bengal's political class mobilised against industrial projects in Singur and Nandigram. Today, many of those political actors either constitute an important part of the new political establishment, or have moved into entirely different political formations.One may celebrate or criticise this phenomenon. But it deserves analysis rather than outrage. The human mind, after all, is a time-variant function. Mathematics teaches us that important variables seldom remain constant. Political preferences are no exception. The objective function of a leader in opposition differs from that of the same leader in government. In electoral democracy, opposition rewards agitation, while government rewards investment; employment and revenue suddenly become governing responsibilities rather than campaign slogans.Consequently, it may be unnecessary to ask whether politicians have become different human beings. The more relevant question is whether the institutional incentives under which they operate have changed.Many of the legal instruments required for assembling industrial land already exist. Creating another set of laws, by itself, will not rebuild West Bengal's industrial land bank. What is required is an unambiguous intention to build industry rather than perform shallow politics. The Left Front came to power in 1977 with a clear intention to pursue land reform for the landless. Today, the era, ideology and people are different. Will the new industrial agenda reflect genuine intent? Or will it be merely political rhetoric?

articles.title: More big names gets SIR notices
articles.summary: External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar, his wife Kyoko S Jaishankar, CBI Director Praveen Sood and former Army Chief General Upendra Dwivedi are among the prominent people who have received notices from the Election Commission (EC) during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Delhi, according to media reports.Sood's wife Vanita Sood and mother Kamlesh Sood, along with Dwivedi's wife Sunita Dwivedi, have also received notices. The wife and son of CPM MP John Brittas are among those served notices during the exercise.Also Read: Delhi SIR: Advani, Sisodia figure in list of voters with 'discrepancies'The notices have been issued in the New Delhi Assembly constituency.Jaishankar and his wife have been placed in the "unmapped with last SIR" category. This means their current electoral records could not be linked with the rolls prepared during the previous revision exercise in 2002.The couple are registered voters in the Sunder Bagh electoral part of the New Delhi Assembly constituency.Sood, his wife and mother have also received notices under the same category. Dwivedi and his wife have been served notices citing the same discrepancy. They are also registered voters in the New Delhi Assembly constituency.Advani and Sisodia also figured on the listFormer deputy prime minister LK Advani, his daughter Pratibha Advani and daughter-in-law Geetika Advani were among those who received notices during the exercise. Advani's name could not be mapped to the 2002 electoral roll, while his son Jayant cleared the mapping exercise.Also Read: Nagaland's draft electoral roll after SIR retains 11.99 lakh voters, excludes 1.59 lakhFormer Delhi deputy chief minister Manish Sisodia, his wife Seema and son Meer also received notices. Sisodia's notice did not specify the reason, while his wife's notice cited a mismatch in her name and his son's notice referred to a discrepancy in his parent's name.Kejriwal and family members received SIR noticesAAP chief and former Delhi Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal, his wife Sunita Kejriwal, son Pulkit Kejriwal and parents Gobind Ram Kejriwal and Gita Devi have also received notices during the SIR exercise.The five family members are registered voters in the New Delhi Assembly constituency. Their names were flagged under the "unmapped with last SIR" category, indicating that their current electoral records could not be linked to the rolls prepared during the previous revision.The Electoral Registration Officer said their enumeration forms did not contain sufficient details to establish the required links with the electoral rolls in their respective states.The notices prompted questions from the AAP over why Kejriwal and his family had been flagged during the exercise.Rekha Gupta's name cleared after verificationDelhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta had also received a notice during the SIR exercise after her electoral details were flagged over an age-related discrepancy involving her and her parents.Following verification of her documents and electoral details, her entry was validated for inclusion in the electoral roll for the Shalimar Bagh Assembly constituency.CEO clarifies notices do not mean deletionDelhi Chief Electoral Officer Ashok Kumar has clarified that receiving a notice during the SIR exercise does not mean a voter's name will be deleted from the electoral roll.The CEO's office said no name can be removed without giving the elector an opportunity to be heard and passing a proper, reasoned and appealable order. It added that system-generated notices are being issued to correct data in ECINET.Electors who receive notices can submit their responses and supporting documents to the concerned Electoral Registration Officer or Booth Level Officer. The prescribed list of documents is indicative and not exhaustive, with decisions to be taken on a case-by-case basis.The notice disposal process is scheduled to conclude by October 29, while the final electoral roll is due to be published on November 4.Meanwhile, Delhi received 84,263 Form 6 applications for inclusion in the electoral roll between August 31 and September 19. Another 2,12,400 applications had been received up to August 30. Form 6 is used to apply for inclusion in the voter list.

articles.title: Fake drugs: Karnataka cancels 16 licenses
articles.summary: Karnataka’s Food Safety and Drug Administration (FDA) has uncovered an alleged unlicensed pharmaceutical repacking and relabelling operation at a farmhouse in Bidadi, with spurious drugs, machinery and printing material worth about Rs 5.05 crore seized during a raid on August 18.The department, which is conducting a series of raids on orders from new Health & Family Welfare Minister UT Khader, has also initiated action against retailers and wholesalers allegedly linked to the distribution and sale of spurious drugs. The licences of 16 entities have been cancelled and those of eight others suspended, according to an FDA statement.The licence of Pfizer C&F Depot at Kempalinganahalli in Nelamangala taluk, Bengaluru Rural district, also figures among the licenses suspended.The FDA's Drug Enforcement Wing conducted the joint inspection following a tip-off at a farmhouse in Kurubarakeranahalli in Bengaluru South district.Preliminary findings suggest the premises were allegedly used to procure low-cost medicines from neighbouring states, repackage them and relabel them as expensive life-saving drugs. The products allegedly carried labels imitating imported products under the Pfizer brand.The FDA said the counterfeit labels included QR and scanning codes that were non-functional when checked. The seized stock is undergoing laboratory analysis to establish its chemical composition, potency and sterility.The operation has raised concerns over the risks posed by unlicensed drug repacking and counterfeit medicines, particularly when products are presented as branded or life-saving drugs. Under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, a drug is spurious if it is an imitation or substitute for another drug, resembles another drug in a manner likely to deceive, or purports to be a manufacturer's product when it is not.The department has registered a criminal case under the Act and is investigating the alleged supply chain. The seized drugs, machinery and printing material will be produced before the jurisdictional JMFC court for further proceedings, according to the FDA statement.The FDA also found 30 boxes of expired medicines at the premises, raising concerns that expired products could have been reintroduced into the supply chain.As part of the investigation, batch numbers and other details of the seized medicines are being blocked on the Karnataka FDA portal to prevent their further sale or distribution. Samples have been sent for testing.The Drugs and Cosmetics Act provides stringent penalties for offences involving spurious drugs, with punishment depending on the nature of the offence and the relevant provision invoked.The FDA has advised consumers to buy medicines only from licensed pharmacies and obtain valid invoices. It has also urged patients and consumers to report suspicious packaging, unusual labelling or non-functional QR codes to drug enforcement authorities.

articles.title: Owaisi open to alliance ahead of UP polls
articles.summary: Lucknow: All India Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen (AIMIM) chief Asaduddin Owaisi on Sunday said that the party is ready to work with those who want to prevent the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) from forming the government in Uttar Pradesh for a third consecutive term, while asserting that the upcoming assembly election in the state will be different from the previous poll.Speaking to about the possibility of an alliance ahead of the UP assembly elections in 2027, Owaisi said that no single party can stop the BJP alone and invited like-minded parties for discussions.Also read: Assembly elections: As polls approach, UP turns into 'katha' pradesh"We do not want the BJP government to be formed for a third time in Uttar Pradesh. If anyone does not want the BJP to form the government, they can talk to us. We are ready to work with you to stop the BJP from coming to power. But it is important to understand that you cannot stop the BJP alone," Owaisi said.Recalling the party's efforts during the Bihar elections, the AIMIM chief said that his party had approached various opposition leaders seeking seats for an alliance, adding that none of them agreed to this."We said this in Bihar as well, and our president, Akhtarul Iman, wrote a letter not just to the RJD or the Congress, but to all the CPI and Communist Party leaders. We said, 'Please give us six seats.' But they did not agree," he said.Owaisi said that AIMIM's organisation has strengthened in Uttar Pradesh and claimed that the party's leadership has emerged from the grassroots level."Our party organisation has become quite strong. Our leadership has emerged at the grassroots level, and our leaders have a strong connection with the ground. The party is working hard on its part," he said.He added that the party would continue its work irrespective of alliance discussions."Whether we are in talks with whom or not is a different matter, but we will continue our work. If you want to stop the BJP, come and talk to us. We are ready to work with you. Now, if they do not want to, that is fine. The people of Uttar Pradesh are watching who wants to stop the BJP and who wants to help it succeed," Owaisi said.Owaisi also said that the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections would not be similar to previous elections and would pose different challenges."Assembly elections are coming. It won't be the 2014 election, nor the 2017 election, nor the 2019 election, nor the 2022 election. This is going to be a completely different election," he said.Targeting the BJP government in Uttar Pradesh, Owaisi alleged that several promises made by the party had not been fulfilled and raised issues related to governance, law and order, electricity and land disputes."This will be a very different election and a very challenging one because the BJP hasn't fulfilled the promises they made," he said.Criticising the previous Samajwadi Party government and the current BJP government, Owaisi said, "When the Samajwadi Party was in power, one kind of hooliganism used to happen. Someone else did it. Now, under their government, a different kind of hooliganism is happening."He also raised questions over the alleged Ram Mandir embezzlement case and sought the release of the SIT report."Why isn't the SIT report released to the public? Why doesn't the government release it? And why are those people getting bail? How are they getting bail? It's strange. This will also be a big talking point," Owaisi said.Talking about AIMIM's preparations for the upcoming elections, Owaisi said that the party has been visiting different constituencies to strengthen its organisation and understand people's issues."In preparation for the upcoming Assembly elections, we have already visited various constituencies in Uttar Pradesh and will continue to do so. Today, we are in Kanpur. In six days, we will be in Shravasti, followed by Azamgarh," he said.He added, "After that, we will hold public meetings in three or four other constituencies in Western Uttar Pradesh. The sole purpose is to strengthen our party organisation for the upcoming elections."Owaisi said that remaining among people helps the party understand their problems on the ground."By staying among the people, we can understand their suffering on the ground and highlight the difficulties this government has created for them," he said.

articles.title: Tata Trusts calls Chandra vote invalid
articles.summary: Tata Trusts has rejected the contention that a casting vote could validate the reappointment of N. Chandrasekaran as chairman of Tata Sons, saying the resolution failed to meet a separate voting requirement under the holding company's articles of association.The Trusts, in a statement on Sunday, said two of their nominees sit on the Tata Sons board and that the articles require affirmative support from a majority of the directors nominated by Tata Trusts, which owns about 66% of the company. One of the two nominees voted against the resolution at the Sept. 17 board meeting, meaning the required support was not secured, it said.Also read: Tata Sons dispute: Abhishek Singhvi says he enters fray with 'sadness and regret'The Trusts disputed the argument that the vote had resulted in a board deadlock that could be resolved by the chairman's casting vote."A condition is either met, or it is not," the Trusts said, arguing that the casting vote applies only when there is an equality of votes at the overall board level and cannot override the separate requirement concerning Tata Trusts' nominees.The Trusts said the resolution to reappoint Chandrasekaran, who has led Tata Sons since 2017, was therefore not validly passed and had no legal effect.The dispute turns on provisions in Tata Sons' articles that give Tata Trusts' nominee directors affirmative voting rights on certain matters. The Trusts said Tata Sons had previously defended those rights before India's Supreme Court during litigation stemming from the removal of former chairman Cyrus Mistry.Tata Sons had argued in that case that the rights were legitimate protections agreed between shareholders and reflected the Trusts' position as the company's majority shareholder, according to the Trusts' statement. The Supreme Court accepted Tata Sons' case and overturned a finding that the provisions were oppressive, the Trusts said.The latest dispute comes as Tata Sons faces renewed scrutiny over its governance and the possibility of a stock-market listing. The Trusts rejected the argument that listing would necessarily strengthen governance, saying Tata Sons had voluntarily adopted several governance practices associated with public companies, including independent directors, audit and nomination committees, related-party transaction rules and insider-trading provisions.Also read: Inside the 24 hours that laid bare Tata’s brutal power struggleThe statement marks a fresh escalation in the disagreement over the governance of India's biggest business group, with the Tata Trusts arguing that the articles themselves provide the framework for resolving the board's decision rather than creating a deadlock requiring intervention by the chairman.The Trusts said their position was rooted in the role they have played in philanthropy for more than 130 years.

of respondents identifying it as the primary benefit.This is followed by stronger employee loyalty at 26 per cent and lower employee attrition at 22 per cent, while 13 per cent see access to untapped talent as the key advantage, it said.According to the report, the manufacturing sector is emerging as one of the biggest beneficiaries of this shift.Around 37 per cent of respondents expect employment expansion."Tier II and III cities are no longer being viewed simply as alternatives to metros; they are increasingly becoming strategic talent markets in their own right. articles.title: India’s cross-border payments need reset
articles.summary: New Delhi: A shift from corridor-led expansion to customer-centric design forms the core principle needed to drive the next stage of India's cross-border payment ecosystem, according to a report by Deloitte.The report outlined that future policy frameworks, digital infrastructure, and regulatory platforms require realignment around distinct user cohorts rather than generic, corridor-focused rollouts."India has built many of the foundational elements of a globally competitive cross-border payments ecosystem. However, the next phase of growth will be determined by the design principles that shape future policy, infrastructure and ecosystem decisions," the report said.As cross-border payments evolve towards always-on, interconnected networks, future policy discussions will sharpen focus on questions beyond payment speed and cost.The Deloitte report mentioned that issues such as the "allocation of fraud liability across jurisdictions, cross-border data sharing and localisation requirements, governance of tokenised settlement networks and mechanisms for supporting real-time beneficiary credit while preserving settlement certainty will play an important role in shaping the next generation of cross-border payment ecosystems."The report noted four central principles to steer this transition. Beyond designing around consumer journeys, the framework calls for making interoperability default across the transaction lifecycle, building an open digital ecosystem with shared infrastructure, and maintaining transparency by default.Specific measures include developing sector-specific payment journeys, establishing differentiated propositions for emerging digital economy participants, and prioritising customer outcomes alongside payment connectivity and transaction processing."India's next phase of cross-border payments should move beyond expanding bilateral payment corridors to designing solutions around the needs of specific customer cohorts. Exporters, MSMEs, gig workers, multinational corporations, travellers and remittance users each face distinct payment, compliance and documentation challenges. Future payments infrastructure, regulatory frameworks and DPI should therefore be designed around customer journeys rather than a one-size-fits-all cross-border payment experience," the report stated.To implement lifecycle interoperability, the report highlighted the integration of payment systems with regulatory bodies such as customs, GST, DGFT, EDPMS, and IDPMS through standardised APIs, reusable digital data, and lower duplicate reporting requirements.Shared infrastructure components also entail expanding API-based access to DPI, creating reusable digital identity and KYC frameworks, and maintaining proportionate, risk-based oversight.Transparency requirements center on standardising fee and foreign exchange margin disclosures, providing end-to-end tracking, and improving settlement predictability."While faster cross-border payments are the objective, the larger emphasis is on creating an ecosystem where exporters can get paid faster, digital earners can participate globally with less friction and remittance users receive more value from every transaction," the report added. "By combining interoperable DPI with coordinated regulation, open ecosystem participation and customer-centric innovation, India can build the digital rails needed to support a USD 1 trillion export economy this year, scale towards USD 2 trillion over the next five years and enable a digital economy projected to contribute nearly 20 percent of GDP by 2030."

articles.title: India’s street food paradox
articles.summary: Every morning at around 8:30, Vijay Raut starts selling his cutting chai in Mahim, Mumbai. Taxi drivers stop for a glass. Construction workers come for a quick cuppa before work. Over the seven years he has been selling tea here, em- ployees from a nearby bank have grown to know him well, and made him the regular supplier of tea, twice a day.For the past month and a half, however, his biggest problem has been finding a place to sell tea. The ramshackle wooden structure from which Raut operated was taken away by the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) during its recent en- forcement drive tackling illegal pavement encroachment.“I eventually got it back after paying a fine of Rs 1,100 apart from bearing the cost of transporting it,” says Raut. But he is afraid of putting it back up. The tea, however, has not disappeared. Nor have his customers, who still need their morning chai. “Now I carry tea in a flask, serving customers for a limited period,” he says. Raut’s wife is eight months pregnant.His father is in intensive care. He has regular customers. But the structure that housed his business is no longer secure because his business is, at the end of the day, illegal. Therein lies a bizarre paradox playing out across cities, from Mumbai to Bengaluru to Thiruvananthapuram. Street food vendors occupy an uneasy place in India’s cities: essential to everyday life, but with little clout.They are housed on foot- paths, which are being reclaimed for pedes- trians. They also carry a reputation for being dirty, which has made them an obvious tar- get of food safety drives. The story of Raut and many like him ex- poses the weakness of a system that has allowed vendors to operate without secure spaces, basic infrastructure and consist- ent oversight. While cities are trying to make public spac- es cleaner and safer, they may be undermining small businesses and affordable food networks for millions. Solving this is critical to designing an inclusive, clean and equitable urban landscape.134363945BIG PLATEIndia has one of the world’s richest street food traditions, ranging from vada pav, medu vada and bhel to golgappa, kebabs to chaat. Street food is cheap, accessible and deeply tied to the cultural identity of cities. For millions, street food is not an occasional indulgence. It is breakfast before a train, a vada pav between shifts, dosa on the way to work, a sandwich at lunchtime, noodles after a late shift, or cutting chai between two meetings.For workers, students, taxi drivers and commuters living on tight budgets, street food solves two problems at once—it is affordable and accessible. It is also an enormous informal economy. The National Association of Street Vendors of India (NASVI) said in 2021 that “10 million vendors in India make up a thriving street vendor market estimated to be at around Rs 8,000 crore daily”.For comparison, Jubilant FoodWorks, one of India’s biggest restaurant companies, reported revenues of Rs 9,512 crore for FY26, which works out to around Rs 26 crore per day. While that establishes the scale of the street food market, it also underlines a key issue. The informal nature of the ecosystem means these vendors work outside the system. That has positives for those who grab grub at these joints, as prices don’t have to factor in compliance. As architect and urban planner Chandrashekhar Prabhu says, “The mo- ment you put them in the formal sector, they have to pay rent, taxes, electricity and water charges, which makes them expensive. The moment they become expensive, they will not be catering to the kind of economic strata they are supposed to cater to.”NEEDED: CLEANLINESSFood safety infra is rarely built into the price either.There are genuine hygiene risks with street food. Lolly Mukesh Jain, professor in the de- partment of microbiology, KJ Somaiya College of Science and Commerce, Mumbai, says street food risks come from contamination, microbial multiplication and survival of microorganisms.Unsafe water, raw ingredients, hands, uten- sils, insects, dust and dirty surfaces can in- troduce contamination. Cooked foods such as rice, gravies, dairy products and chutneys become particularly vulnerable when kept for long periods at room temperature. But Jain says the location of food is not what determines safety. With basic infra- structure and training, she says, a well- designed street food stall can achieve food safety standards comparable to a small restaurant.A street food stall does not need a restau- rant-style kitchen. It needs potable water, soap-based handwashing facilities, clean utensils and surfaces, separation of raw and cooked food and temperature control. India’s food safety regulator, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), already has hygiene require- ments for small food operators and street food vendors. Its Clean Street Food pro- gramme focuses on training and capacity- building alongside regulation. From April 1 this year, FSSAI’s revised li- censing framework also raised the annual turnover threshold for basic food business registration from Rs 12 lakh to Rs 1.5 crore. In theory, this should reduce compliance costs for small businesses.In 2025, FSSAI said it had worked with BMC to train more than 4,000 street vendors, self- help groups and mid-day meal providers, as part of an initiative targeting 10,000 vendors across Mumbai. Vendors who are registered under the Street Vendors Act through municipal corporations or town vending committees are deemed registered under the FSSAI framework, subject to hygiene and sanitary requirements. But most of this remains on paper.WHOSE SPACE IS IT?There is another unresolved question: Who has the legal right to oc- cupy public space? Prabhu points out, “Footpaths are for pe- destrians, not ven- dors.” He talks about spaces like Nariman Point in Mumbai which, when it was planned, did not have any space for vendors. “Then a decision was taken to keep some space behind the Air India building for peo- ple to have street food.” But such places are rare, and vendors across India end up occupying pedes-trian space.The Street Vendors (Protection of Livelihood and Regulation of Street Vending) Act, 2014, does provide a frame- work for recognising and regulating ven- dors. “But Mumbai’s street-vending system is still struggling to fully implement it,” says a person close to vendor licensing, who didn’t want to come on the record. Queries sent to BMC and FSSAI went unanswered. Simply put, regulation without infra- structure can push vendors further into informality, not eliminate problems.LOOK EAST FOR ANSWERSItalian chef Adriano Baldassarre, who has a Michelin-starred restaurant, Tordomatto, in Rome, has fond memories of Indian street food. He spent nearly 12 years in India and also worked as a private chef for the Ambani family. He recalls eat- ing chaat on Delhi’s streets and ap- preciates their authentic- ity. His most vivid memory is being served samosas in a newspaper.Hygiene remains a concern. But for Baldassarre, the answer is not to eliminate street food. Vendors, he believes, “can be better sup- ported to improve hygiene while retaining the authentic- ity and taste that make Indian street food distinctive”.Is there a way out? Looking East would be a good starting point. Across most of Asia, from Japan and China to Taiwan, Thailand and Singapore, street food is an important part of the urban fabric. Even Singapore, with limited real estate and high cleanliness quotient, did not eliminate its hawker culture in the name of hygiene. It instead moved vendors into regu- lated, purpose-built centres with water, drainage, waste management and other ba- sic facilities.As Andrew Tam wrote in an article in Gastronomica, “Hawking in Singapore was initially seen as a nuisance that had to be tolerated and later regulated by both the colonial administration and newly in- dependent government. The relocation of hawkers to centralized food centers marked the imposition of order and hy- giene onto a squalid industry.”Malaysia has similarly developed hawker centres and food courts, while Vietnam has experimented with designated areas and food safety oversight. Street food in many of these cities is a legit tourist attraction. So much so that the purveyor of great grub, the Michelin Guide, has a specific recognition, Bib Gourmand, for such eateries. Michelin says the approach demonstrates that “quality is not defined by the setting, but by the food itself”, and that exceptional cuisine can be found “from street stalls and neighbourhood eateries to some of the world’s most renowned restaurants”. Singapore’s hawker culture, it says, is a strong example.The reality is that the demand for street food is not going away. India will continue to eat on its streets. The question is whether its vendors will still have a place there, says Baldassarre. India cannot simply copy global models. Its streets are more crowded, its vending economy more informal and its history different. But the comparison raises the possibility that regulation does not necessarily have to mean disappearance.India’s challenge is therefore larger than ensuring a chai seller, sandwich maker, or noodle vendor has a licence. “It is whether the city can create a system in which street food is safer without making the people who sell it invisible,” says Baldassarre.SURVIVAL MODEFor now, vendors are in survival mode. Vinita Shinde once sold Chinese food from a makeshift stall in Dadar in Central Mumbai, working from morning till 11 at night. On a single stove, she prepared noodles, manchurian and fried rice, tossing vegetables and tur ning out orders. She was the only earning member in her family. Her routine has changed over the past few weeks: “I am preparing a few dishes closer home and serving customers for just two-three hours.”Her business continues, but at a much smaller scale. Then there is Manjunath Shirodkar, a sandwich seller from Prabhadevi in south Mumbai. For years, he sat at a familiar spot facing the main road. “Now I prepare chutney and vegetables at home, carry them to the old location, serve my regular customers and leave in a jiffy,” says Shirodkar. The vendors make less money because they don’t have the space they used to. To meet household expenses, including his wife’s medical costs, Shirodkar has start- ed delivering vegetables and milk in the morning and evening.A coconut-water seller near Dadar has found another workaround. After being moved from his regular spot, he now brings a few coconuts and sits inside a nearby shoe shop, where regular clients come looking for him. He charges a premium, but customers continue to buy. For years, say vendors, enforcement was something they negotiated around. Carts would be seized, fines paid and businesses resumed. Some say they rou- tinely paid enforcement officials to keep selling from their spots. Now, they say, it feels different.

Elavenil Valarivan, Sonam Maskar and Vidarsa Vinod combined for a total of 1898.0 points to finish second behind China, who topped the standings with a world-record score of 1904.2.
Hosts Japan finished third with 1897.1 points.
This is India's first confirmed medal at the Aichi-Nagoya 20th Asian Games.
MMA fighter Suchika Tariyal was the first Indian athlete to assure a medal, reaching the women's Traditional MMA 60kg semifinals.
Sonam was India's top scorer with 634.1 points, followed by Elavenil with 633.5 and Vidarsa with 630.4.
Elavenil and Sonam also qualified for the individual final, with their scores placing them among the finalists.
Elavenil and Sonam will look for a double in the eight-woman individual final to be held later in the day.
